paragraphs: I design brand identities and build products at the intersection of design and technology.
intro.companiesLabel: Products I've made are used by people at:

work.title: sort.cash
work.description: A consumer budgeting app I design and build end to end, teaching financial literacy on the way to a funded emergency account.

body: A budgeting app that teaches financial literacy in the flow of using it. Income runs through a fixed sequence of priorities, savings first, and the product hands back a single figure: what is safe to spend. The target state is a funded emergency account, not an engaged user.

Finder found that 43% of Australians hold less than $1,000 in their bank account, and that inside that group the average balance is $215.1 The advice that fixes it is not scarce. It is the most repeated advice in personal finance. What is scarce is the bridge between knowing and doing, and most budgeting apps are built for the far side of it. They open onto categories, charts and reconciliation, and they assume the person reading those things already knows what the numbers mean and what to do when one of them is too high. Financial literacy is treated as a prerequisite rather than as something the product might supply.

I built this because I was on the near side of that bridge myself: debt, no plan, and no vocabulary for any of it. sort.cash is for people in their twenties and early thirties who are earning properly for the first time and have never held a budget.

The engine is two old ideas. Income falls through an ordered sequence rather than into a grid of categories that all compete at once, and savings sit at the top of the fall instead of at the bottom where the leftovers land. The proportions come from The Richest Man in Babylon: a tenth of everything you earn is yours to keep, before it is anyone else’s.2 Together they produce the product’s only real output, a spend figure that is permitted rather than merely remaining. The user does not decide to save. They decide how to spend what is left after saving already happened.

Two things follow from that. There are no bank connections, so everything stays local and the user sets their own numbers, which means the gap between what they guessed their bills were and what the bills turn out to be is the first thing the product teaches them. And no figure appears without the arithmetic that produced it, because someone who has never budgeted does not need a more authoritative number. They need to see that the number comes from their own behaviour, and that changing the behaviour changes it.

It does not police anyone. No overspend alarms, no streaks, no notifications asking where you have been. Guilt ends the relationship with the tool, and a tool nobody opens is worth nothing, so the product notifies about the state of an object and never about the conduct of a person. A figure that has gone six months without review is a fact about the figure.

I design and build it end to end: vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript inside Tauri 2, iOS first, with the brand, the waiting list and a working MVP done and a TestFlight build next. That part has been the most useful design education I have had. Designing and building the same screen removes the option of hand-waving, and the screens easiest to skip in a design file, the empty state and the error and the moment a real balance arrives lower than expected, are exactly the ones that have to exist in a build.

caseStudy.heading: Cites
body: 1 Finder, Breaking point: 9.2 million Aussies have less than $1,000 in savings, June 2025. Consumer Sentiment Tracker, 1,310 respondents, May 2025 wave. finder.com.au/news/breaking-point-2025
2 George S. Clason, The Richest Man in Babylon, 1926. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Richest_Man_in_Babylon

work.title: Casey Stevenson
work.description: A site and identity for an actor — one place for his work, his portraits, and the way to reach him.
work.caseStudy: Casey Stevenson is an actor, and my cousin. He needed one place to market his work, show his portraits, and be contacted from. I designed and built the site and the identity behind it. The identity stays deliberately minimal: an actor this early is still working out what he is on screen, and a look that commits hard now is one that has to be undone later. What's here is a foundation — type, spacing, and a way of framing the portraits — with room to carry more as his career does.

work.title: Hnry
work.description: A concept rebrand for Hnry, maturing its circular H glyph and making invoicing and expense flows more explicit.

images.caption: App concept — invoicing and expense tracking flows.

work.caseStudy: A redesign of the Hnry brand that respectfully preserves the iconic circular 'H' glyph while maturing it for a more modern feel. The refreshed identity introduces a subtly expanded color palette for a more vibrant, forward-thinking look. On the product side, several app screens were updated to make key flows — like invoicing and expense tracking — more explicit and intuitive, honoring Hnry's evolving brand while staying true to its roots.

work.title: Engulf Studio
work.description: My own web3-centric design practice, spanning brand identity, art direction, UX/UI, web and app work.
work.caseStudy: Engulf Studio is my own independent design practice (currently on hiatus) — a web3-centric studio spanning brand identity, art direction, UX/UI, web, and app work. It's where I take on projects that let me push further creatively than client work usually allows.

work.title: Pinetree
work.description: Design across a web3 video platform's screens, from landing pages and onboarding to subscriptions and live transcription.
work.caseStudy: Pinetree, formerly Netbox, was a groundbreaking startup in the web3 space, offering a video-sharing platform in the spirit of YouTube. Brought on for design, I worked across the web app's screens — crafting landing pages, onboarding flows, subscription flows, a trending section, and a live-transcription feature. Each screen was designed to lift engagement and deliver a stronger user experience, blending familiar video-platform conventions with web3-native features.

work.title: Northbound Gear
work.description: A brand platform and identity refresh for an outdoor apparel label, carried across packaging, landing pages, apparel and social.

images.caption: Beanie design, carrying the refreshed identity on a woven label.

work.caseStudy: Northbound Gear is an outdoor apparel label. Working remotely with founder Sunny Gosal, I developed the Onwards & Upwards brand platform and the refreshed identity that sits on it, then took it across everything it had to live on: print and packaging collateral, landing pages, the apparel itself, and social ads. The clearest result came from the smallest object — a beanie, designed to the new identity, that went on to drive over $24,000 CAD in revenue.

work.title: VTNZ
work.description: Customer-facing marketing for a vehicle inspection network, across print, digital, social, email and motion.
work.caseStudy: Working closely with the Marketing and Product Development leads, I helped create customer-facing marketing materials across print, digital advertising, social media, email, videography, motion graphics, templates, and on-location screen advertising. The accompanying logo redesign shown here was a personal concept explored in my own time, not an official VTNZ rebrand.

work.title: healthCar
work.description: Brand identity for a VTNZ and Provident Insurance sub-brand, covering guidelines, typography and product mockups.
work.caseStudy: healthCar is a sub-brand partnership between VTNZ and Provident Insurance. I led the brand identity development — creating brand guidelines, choosing typography, building app and website mockups, and designing a logo from sketches through more than 30 iterations. Collaborating with Catch Design on the website and logo gave me valuable insight into how agencies approach design.

work.title: Warchest
work.description: A concept financial analytics product, exploring interface and brand design in the spirit of Baremetrics, Stripe and Uphold.
work.caseStudy: Warchest is a concept financial analytics product, inspired by the UI and brand identity of SaaS companies like Baremetrics, Stripe, and Uphold. A personal exploration in interface and brand design outside of client work.

work.title: Rebels And Rebellions
work.description: A concept top-shelf liquor brand translating the rebellious streak of the American Revolution into contemporary luxury.
work.caseStudy: Rebels And Rebellions is a concept top-shelf liquor brand. Its identity draws on the rebellious American attitude of the American Revolution, the Whiskey Rebellion, and the Boston Tea Party, translated into a contemporary luxury aesthetic.

work.title: Eight360
work.description: A brand and web overhaul for a virtual reality motion company, extending into demo content for its flagship NOVA platform.
work.caseStudy: Eight360 is a virtual reality motion company founded by Terry Miller and George Heather-Smith. They brought me on to overhaul their brand identity and web design, and eventually to create demo content for their flagship NOVA motion platform.

work.title: Secret Kings
work.description: A personal brand built on Instagram to over 16,000 followers, teaching me micro-brand marketing and business strategy.
work.caseStudy: Secret Kings is a personal concept I've worked on since May 2015. Built on Instagram, the project grew an audience of over 16,000 followers at its peak. It taught me micro-brand marketing, business strategy, and copywriting — skills well beyond design.

work.title: Signal
work.description: A VR experience pairing print with cross-reality asymmetrical multiplayer, set in an early-80s take on mystery.
work.caseStudy: Signal is a virtual reality experience using storytelling to explore mystery, nostalgia, and evolving technology. Combining print and VR, it challenges biased perceptions of VR through cross-reality asymmetrical multiplayer gameplay with an early-80s aesthetic. Within the story, Universe Amalgamation Systems (UAS) makes parallel universes accessible to all lifeforms, and the player group Monarch must take down a corrupt faction within it.

work.title: Tesla
work.description: A final-year rebrand exploring how a company's image and identity can be brought in line with its core principles.
work.caseStudy: This Tesla rebrand was an assignment for an Image & Identity class in my final year of university. The project explored the fundamentals of how brands function in terms of image and identity, and how to portray a brand in line with its core principles and aims.

posts.title: Elon Musk Stole My Meme
posts.summary: Between August 2023 and the middle of 2024 I went from around 600 followers to over 2,000, sold merch into Silicon Valley, Japan and Canada, and had one of my images reposted by Elon Musk to 45 million people.

body: Between August 2023 and the middle of 2024 I went from around 600 followers to over 2,000, sold merch into Silicon Valley, Japan and Canada, and had one of my images reposted by Elon Musk to 45 million people. For most of that period I was working part-time in the flooring department of a Mitre 10 Mega in Wellington, cutting fake grass and lifting heavy tiles.
None of it came from a portfolio, a pitch, or an application. It came from a single idea I picked up in a community called Visualize Value, run by Jack Butcher: permissionless apprenticeship.1

body.heading: The mechanic
body: The premise is simple enough to explain in one sentence. You do the work for someone without being asked, publish it, tag them, and see what happens.

No brief, no invoice, no request for a meeting. You identify someone doing interesting work, find the gap between what they have and what they should have, close it, and put it in public. The output has to be genuinely good for them, not for you. That's the whole discipline.

What you're actually doing is engineering luck surface area. Opportunity arrives in proportion to how much of your work is visible and how many people it's visible to. Most people sit inside a closed system: their work goes to a client, the client approves it, nobody else ever sees it. Permissionless work punches a hole in that system and attaches your name to someone with far more exposure than you have. You are not asking for a share of their audience. You are giving them something worth showing to it.

body.heading: e/acc
body: In August 2023 the effective accelerationism movement was forming on X.2 It was being driven largely by two anonymous accounts, Beff Jezos and bayeslord, who were writing the founding material for the ideology in public.
They had ideas and no visual identity. So I made them one: profile pictures and profile covers for both accounts, unprompted, and posted them.

figures.alt: Profile cover designed for @basedbeffjezos: a hulking figure standing on an orange Martian plain in front of industrial machinery, with BASEDBEFFJEZOS set in chrome lettering across the top
figures.caption: Profile cover made for @basedbeffjezos, unprompted, August 2023.

figures.alt: Profile cover designed for @bayeslord: an armoured eagle figure standing in a dense retrofuturist megacity, with BAYESLORD set in yellow lettering across the top
figures.caption: Profile cover for @bayeslord, from the same run.

body: They followed me. They reposted the work. That was the door.

Beff Jezos was later revealed as Guillaume Verdon, who went on to found Extropic, building chips that use the analogue noise of physics itself to run probabilistic inference rather than forcing everything through deterministic ones and zeros.3 That is the calibre of person the community was full of, which is worth stating plainly: these were not shitposters. They were extremely bright people who happened to communicate through memes.

body.heading: The store
body: On 20 September 2023 I posted a mockup of a black hoodie with ANTI DECEL EACC CLUB across the chest, captioned as nothing more than an idea, and tagged Beff, bayeslord and xlr8harder. There was no product behind it. No store, no supplier, no stock. It was a render.

figures.alt: Tyler's post of a black hoodie mockup reading ANTI DECEL EACC CLUB, captioned as an idea
figures.caption: The original post, 20 September 2023. No store, no supplier, no stock.

body: Less than two hours later Garry Tan replied with the Fry GIF. Shut up and take my money.

figures.alt: Garry Tan's reply: the Futurama Fry GIF captioned shut up and take my money
figures.caption: Garry Tan's reply, less than two hours later.

body: Then he did the thing that actually changed the trajectory. He tagged Fourthwall and Walker Williams in the same thread and asked “can we make this happen pls?”

figures.alt: Garry Tan tagging Fourthwall and Walker Williams asking if they can make it happen, with Tyler replying with a store link
figures.caption: The tag that became the entire Fourthwall chapter.

body: I stood up a Shopify store that afternoon and replied with a link. Got you fam.

That tag is the entire Fourthwall chapter. Garry Tan introduced me to Walker Williams, Fourthwall's co-founder, in public, in a reply, to a mockup of a product that did not exist. I later moved the whole store off Shopify onto Fourthwall with help from the people who built it. Garry Tan bought a piece. Will Depue from OpenAI came through.

Over that stretch I made $4,445.40 USD (about $7,650 NZD) in merch sales, shipping to Silicon Valley, Japan, Canada, and a handful of places I had to look up. It taught me more about e-commerce, positioning and marketing than any course would have, because every lesson cost me real money or made me real money.
I typeset Marc Andreessen's Techno-Optimist Manifesto into a proper book, essentially a designed edition of the blog post, and someone at Daylight Computer downloaded a copy.4

body.heading: Ten minutes
body: The meme happened on 20 November 2023, in the middle of the OpenAI weekend. Sam Altman had just been fired, nobody knew who was running the company, and the entire timeline was refreshing itself into a stupor.5 I got home from a shift on the floor, tiles and carpet and offcuts, and opened X.

Aravind Srinivas, the founder of Perplexity, posted the meme, the one where he's staring down the barrel of the camera with a fistful of lit cigarettes bunched together in front of his face. Two words: me right now.

figures.alt: Aravind Srinivas posting the Matthew McConaughey cigarettes frame captioned Me right now, 20 November 2023
figures.caption: Aravind Srinivas's post, 20 November 2023, mid-OpenAI weekend.

body: Someone in the replies pointed out that the cluster of filters looked like an engine array. That was the whole setup, sitting there unassembled.

So I assembled it. I turned the bundle of cigarettes into Starship's Raptor cluster and lit the plume underneath it, so McConaughey is holding a full static fire between his fingers. Ten minutes in Photoshop, posted, done. It did fine on my account, maybe a hundred likes.

Five days later, on 25 November, Elon Musk posted it himself. One word and an emoji: “Starship 🚬”. No credit, no tag. Forty-five million views, just under half a million likes, thirty-nine thousand reposts.

figures.alt: Elon Musk's post of the meme, captioned Starship with a cigarette emoji, showing 45M views, 490K likes and 39K reposts
figures.caption: Elon Musk's post, 25 November 2023. Forty-five million views, no credit.

body: The man who became the first trillionaire ran my ten-minute Photoshop job in front of more people than will ever see anything else I make. I genuinely don't care that he took it. It's funny as hell, and it's better street cred than an award.

body.heading: The hard tech meme machine
body: I kept going. Anduril had just announced the Roadrunner, so I photoshopped Uber Eats livery onto it, purely because the colourway would look sick.6 This was before the image models could do it for you, so it was real compositing work. Palmer Luckey engaged with the post.
On 2 December, Christian Keil, at the time chief of staff at Astranis, posted both memes side by side, said he was buying stock in me early, and called me a “one-man hard-tech meme machine”.

figures.alt: Christian Keil's post showing the Starship meme and the Uber Eats Roadrunner side by side, calling Tyler a one-man hard-tech meme machine
figures.caption: Christian Keil's post, 2 December 2023.

body: I ran with that label for a good while, because a positioning statement handed to you by someone inside one of the most interesting space companies in the world is worth more than one you write for yourself.
For roughly a year I was a small micro-celebrity in Silicon Valley, while my actual job title was flooring team member.

body.heading: What it's actually worth
body: The follower count was never the asset. The asset was proof that the mechanic works.

Taste plus speed plus publishing, applied without permission, gets you into rooms that credentials do not. I had no network in that world, no referral, no relevant employment history. I had the ability to see what a scene needed visually and the willingness to make it before anyone asked. That is a repeatable process, not a lucky run.

The other thing it proved is that the gap between working a retail shift and having your work in front of Marc Andreessen is not a career ladder. It's a single act of publishing, repeated until something lands.
Most people are one permissionless piece of work away from a completely different set of options. They just keep waiting to be picked.

body.heading: Cites
body: 1 Jack Butcher, Permissionless Apprenticeship, Visualize Value. visualizevalue.com/concepts/permissionless-apprenticeship
2 Effective accelerationism, Wikipedia. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_accelerationism

3 Guillaume Verdon, Wikipedia. Verdon wrote as BasedBeffJezos and co-founded Extropic, which builds hardware that computes with probabilistic bits rather than deterministic ones; Forbes identified him in December 2023. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Verdon
4 Marc Andreessen, The Techno-Optimist Manifesto, Andreessen Horowitz, October 2023. a16z.com/the-techno-optimist-manifesto

about: I'm Tyler Pixel (legally Tyler Patterson), a design engineer working across brand and product. Nine years in, I still care most about the thing I cared about on day one: context. Why something exists, who it's for, and what it has to do, long before it needs to look like anything.

I studied Visual Communication Design at Massey University's College of Creative Arts in Wellington, graduating with honours. Since then: identity, interaction, ecommerce, apparel, art direction and packaging. In-house at VTNZ, Eight360 and Northbound Gear. Agency and freelance at Rise SEO, and through my own studio. Between them I learned both halves of the job: the craft and the constraints.

These days I'm in Brisbane, designing and building sort.cash, a budgeting app that teaches financial literacy by getting people to an emergency fund. Building my own product has made me better at designing other people's: it's much harder to hand-wave a decision when you're the one shipping it.
Away from that I make synthwave-leaning music and art as Timecodec, fly FPV drones, and 3D print things I probably don't need.
